description:
We are Team Rudra, a group of passionate and enthusiastic young innovators interested in space, science, technology, and problem-solving. We believe that creativity, teamwork, and innovation can turn great ideas into meaningful solutions.

Our goal is to explore real-world challenges, think beyond limits, and develop innovative ideas inspired by space science and NASA's open data. We are eager to learn new technologies, share knowledge, and work together to create something impactful.
summary: The topic “Abandoned but Not Forgotten – Storytelling About NASA's Discarded Equipment on the Moon and Mars” focuses on the problem of space equipment left behind during NASA's missions to the Moon and Mars. These objects include spacecraft components, landing systems, parachutes, heat shields and scientific instruments. Although they are important parts of space exploration history, information about their locations, conditions and mission purposes is scattered across different records and images. This can make it difficult for future missions to identify these objects, plan safe exploration routes and preserve historically important sites. To address this problem, we propose a system called Lunar & Martian Legacy Tracker (LMLT), an intelligent digital platform that uses Artificial Intelligence (AI), image recognition and interactive 3D mapping to identify, locate and document abandoned space equipment. It will collect available NASA mission images and datasets, classify identified objects, maintain their mission history and display their known locations on a digital map. The system will also help future space missions understand potential hazards and protect important historical sites. The main objective of this project is to connect past space exploration with future missions by making sure that the equipment left behind on the Moon and Mars is properly identified, documented and never forgotten.
details:
What does the project do or how does it work?

Our project, Lunar & Martian Legacy Tracker (LMLT), is an intelligent digital platform designed to identify, locate, document and track abandoned equipment left behind during NASA missions to the Moon and Mars. It works by collecting publicly available NASA mission images and datasets and using Artificial Intelligence (AI) and image recognition techniques to identify objects such as parachutes, spacecraft components, heat shields and landing systems. The identified objects are classified and stored in a centralized database along with their mission details, known locations and historical information. An interactive digital map displays these objects, helping users explore and understand the equipment left behind.

What benefits does it have?

The project provides several benefits, including better documentation of abandoned space equipment, easier access to mission information and improved awareness of human activities on the Moon and Mars. It helps researchers and future mission planners identify previously documented objects and consider their locations while planning exploration routes. It also supports the preservation of historically important space exploration sites and provides an educational platform for students and space enthusiasts.

What is the intended impact of the project?

The main intended impact is to make future space exploration more organized, informed and sustainable. The project aims to connect past space missions with future exploration by preserving information about equipment left behind. It can help researchers understand the history of planetary exploration, reduce uncertainty about known objects and encourage responsible exploration of the Moon and Mars. In the long term, the platform could become a useful digital archive for lunar and Martian mission heritage.

Tools, coding languages, hardware or software we used to develop our project

The proposed project uses Python as the primary programming language, OpenCV for image processing, and Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning techniques for object identification. Publicly available NASA images and datasets are used as the main data sources. A database is used to store equipment information, while GIS tools and 3D visualization software help display object locations on interactive planetary maps. A computer or laptop is sufficient for developing and testing the initial software prototype. No special space hardware is required for the initial version.

How our project is creative

The creativity of our project lies in combining Artificial Intelligence, image recognition, interactive mapping and historical storytelling into a single platform. Instead of treating abandoned equipment as useless space debris, our project gives every identified object a digital identity containing its mission history, location and scientific or historical importance. Users can explore the Moon and Mars through an interactive map and discover the stories behind the objects left by earlier missions. This makes space exploration history more accessible while supporting future scientific activities.

Factors considered by our team

Our team considered several important factors while developing this idea, including the accuracy of object identification, availability and reliability of NASA datasets, location verification, technical feasibility, development cost and ease of use. We also considered the safety of future space missions, preservation of historically important locations, environmental responsibility and the possibility of expanding the system as new mission data becomes available. Since some object locations and conditions may be uncertain, the system should clearly distinguish verified information from AI-generated predictions.

Project's central message:

"Every object left on the Moon and Mars tells a story. Our project aims to preserve those stories while helping future generations explore space more responsibly."
